..
Issued at 1142 PM CDT Tue Aug 11 2026

Main story in the short term is severe storm potential 
overnight into early Wednesday morning. As of 11 PM, ongoing 
storms over southwest SD were pushing southeast and producing 
70+ mph wind gusts in some locations. Looking at the environment
ahead of said storms, there is plenty of instability in place 
(4000+ J/kg of MUCAPE per SPS objective mesoanalysis) along with
plenty of effective and deep layer shear to remain organized. 
0-3 km shear does taper off farther southeast, so assuming 
storms get here, they could become a little more outflow 
dominant. That said, guidance does suggest 0-3 km shear 
strengthens, or at least maintains as we go through the 
overnight hours. Things working against the storms maintaining 
are a little bit of dry air aloft and the primary forcing 
sliding by just to our north. However, with low level moisture 
transport pointing into our area, an already unstable airmass in
place, and latest short-term guidance being in fairly good 
agreement that they make it to and through the area, think we 
will have a severe weather threat starting around 3-4 AM. The 
primary threat will be pockets of 50 to isolated 70+ mph gusts 
and perhaps some hail. In addition, precipitable water values 
around 1.75" and warm cloud depths over 4 km suggest they'll be 
efficient rain producers and could lead to some localized 
flooding, but guidance does suggest they should be somewhat 
progressive. The big questions will be how far south the wind 
threat extends and just how strong the winds will be. Some 
guidance suggests areas as far south as I-80 could see damaging 
winds, while other solutions favor the threat remaining mainly 
in northeast NE and west-central IA. Finally, one thing to watch
is how ongoing weaker storms in north-central NE evolve. For 
now, they seem weak enough that they won't put much of a dent in
the instability in place. However, if they strengthen, they 
could work the environment over just enough that the incoming 
storms from SD end up sub-severe.

Whatever storms do move through should exit to the southeast by
8-9 AM with perhaps a few lingering showers in southeast NE and
far southwest IA along the the surface boundary and any remnant
outflow. With the boundary to the south, we'll be a bit 
"cooler," but still warm and muggy, with highs in the upper 80s 
to lower 90s and dewpoints in the 70s. By late 
afternoon/evening, we should start to see storms develop across 
western NE as shortwave energy currently over the Desert 
Southwest rounds the ridge and pushes into the area. In the low 
levels, a low will push east out of CO and into KS, helping to 
induce a strengthening low level jet/moisture transport that 
runs over the surface boundary near the NE/KS border and points 
into the area. Expect storm development on the nose of this 
moisture transport, with latest CAMs suggesting they'll be 
mostly north of I- 80. That said, it may be worth watching for 
development a little farther south/closer to the surface 
boundary where 900 mb moisture transport points into very strong
frontogenesis. Model soundings suggest there will be a little 
CIN to overcome for parcels originating at that level, but given
the forcing, think it's possible for that CIN to be overcome. 
Regardless of where storms develop, deep layer shear looks 
favorable for storm organization with plenty of instability to 
work with for a damaging wind and hail threat. In addition, 
guidance hints at precipitable water values of 1.75 to 2+ inches
with warm cloud depths of 4+ km, suggesting potential for heavy
rain. With CAMs indicating potential for storms training from 
west to east, a flooding threat could develop into early 
Thursday morning.

Precip should taper off through the morning hours with 
lingering cloud cover across much of the area limiting 
temperatures to the mid 70s to mid 80s, except for near the 
NE/KS/IA/MO border area, where a few lower 90s will be possible.
Rinse, repeat with evening shower and storm chances once again 
as shortwave energy slides through and we see more warm air 
advection, while the surface boundary remains in/near the area. 
While there will be slightly less instability and shear, there 
could be just enough of both to yield at least some stronger 
storms. This pattern with nightly (strong/severe?) storm chances
continues into the weekend before ensemble consensus shows 
surface high pressure building in on Sunday with the surface 
boundary finally pushing well south of our area. However, any 
break we get looks short-lived as guidance hints that the train 
of shortwaves returns into next week with more on and off precip
chances. Otherwise, temperatures remain steady through 
Saturday, before cooler high pressure pushes in and leads to 
highs in the mid 70s to lower/mid 80s Sunday and Monday. 
Temperatures should warm slightly through the rest of the week, 
though will depend on timing of those precip chances.
